lead: This unit follows one artificial neuron from its biological inspiration to a deep network trained on images and sequences. After it you can write the McCulloch–Pitts and perceptron rules, size a multilayer network, derive a backpropagation gradient by hand, and explain convolution, pooling and recurrence well enough to answer a full exam question.
about: Unit 5 builds a network one layer at a time. 5.1 starts with the McCulloch–Pitts neuron, a weighted sum followed by a threshold. 5.2 makes those weights learnable with the perceptron rule and shows where a single layer fails. 5.3 adds hidden layers, 5.4 covers activation and loss functions, and 5.5 derives backpropagation. 5.6 adds optimizers, regularization and dropout, then 5.7 explains depth, saturation and ReLU. 5.8 moves to convolution and pooling in CNNs, and 5.9 closes with recurrent networks and LSTM for sequences. The running thread is always the same: how the network computes an output, and how training changes its weights.

chapters.idea: A neuron adds up weighted inputs and fires only when the total crosses a threshold, so a single unit already computes a logical function.
chapters.depth: The biological parts (dendrite, soma, axon, synapse) only as a naming table, then the McCulloch–Pitts (MP) unit in full: inputs x₁ … xₙ, weights wᵢ, bias b, net input Σwᵢxᵢ + b, output y = 1 if net ≥ θ else 0. Show that with hand-set weights one MP unit is AND, OR or NOT, and that weights are fixed, not learned. Mention the step function name and the bias-as-negative-threshold rewrite y = step(Σwᵢxᵢ − θ).

figure.title: McCulloch–Pitts unit computing AND
figure.aria: Two inputs of weight 1 are added and the result is compared with a threshold of 2 to produce the output.

chapters.example: Build AND with one MP unit: inputs (x₁, x₂), weights w₁ = w₂ = 1, bias b = 0, threshold θ = 2. Check all four rows. (0,0): sum = 0 < 2 → y = 0. (0,1): sum = 1 < 2 → y = 0. (1,0): sum = 1 < 2 → y = 0. (1,1): sum = 2 ≥ 2 → y = 1. Now change θ to 1 and the same unit computes OR. Change w₁ to −1, w₂ to 0 and θ to 0 and it computes NOT x₁.
chapters.trap: The MP unit has no learning step: you set the weights by hand, so it cannot adjust itself from data. Also settle whether the rule is ≥ θ or > θ, and remember the bias counts as a weight on a constant input of 1.
chapters.prereq: None; basic algebra and the idea of a function from Unit 1 help.
chapters.leave: How weights are found automatically is chapter 5.2; gradient descent is Unit 2.

chapters.idea: The perceptron learning rule changes weights only when the unit makes an error, and it converges only when the classes can be split by a straight line.
chapters.depth: Perceptron output model (weighted sum, step, sometimes sign), the update wᵢ ← wᵢ + η(t − y)xᵢ and b ← b + η(t − y), with η the learning rate, t the target and y the output. Cover the error-correction view, the perceptron convergence theorem (finite steps if the data is linearly separable), and the failure cases: XOR, the classic linearly inseparable pattern, and the fact that the boundary is a single straight line (a hyperplane). Mention the pocket or averaged variant only in one line.

figure.title: Perceptron learning cycle
figure.aria: A sample enters, the perceptron computes its output, and if the output is wrong the weights are updated and the sample is tested again.

chapters.example: One update on AND. Start w₁ = w₂ = 0, b = 0, η = 1. Sample (1,1) with target t = 1: net = 0, y = 0, error = t − y = 1, so w₁ = 0 + 1×1×1 = 1, w₂ = 1, b = 0 + 1×1 = 1. Next sample (1,0) with t = 0: net = 1×1 + 1×0 + 1 = 2 ≥ 0 → y = 1, error = −1, so w₁ = 1 + (−1)(1) = 0, w₂ = 1 + (−1)(0) = 1, b = 1 + (−1) = 0. The boundary has moved after two samples.
chapters.trap: XOR cannot be learned by one perceptron no matter how long you train, so do not claim convergence there. Also use the error (t − y) with the right sign; flipping the signs makes the weights run away.
chapters.leave: Logistic regression and the sigmoid version are Unit 2; margin theory is Unit 3 (SVM).

chapters.idea: Adding one or more hidden layers lets a network build intermediate features, so it can represent functions a single layer cannot, such as XOR.
chapters.depth: Architecture vocabulary: input layer, hidden layer(s), output layer, fan-in, fan-out, fully connected (dense), depth versus width. Forward computation layer by layer, a = σ(Wa_prev + b). Parameter counting including biases. Universal approximation in one line (one hidden layer with enough units can approximate a continuous function) and why depth still helps. Show XOR with two hidden units. Some syllabi call this the multilayer perceptron or MLP.

figure.title: 2–3–1 feedforward network
figure.aria: Two inputs feed three hidden units, which feed one output unit, with the numbers of weights and biases marked on each connection block.

chapters.example: Network 2–3–1 with biases: the input-to-hidden link has 2×3 = 6 weights plus 3 biases = 9 parameters; the hidden-to-output link has 3×1 = 3 weights plus 1 bias = 4 parameters; total 13. Now solve XOR with two hidden units and step activation: h₁ = step(x₁ + x₂ − 0.5) (OR), h₂ = step(x₁ + x₂ − 1.5) (AND), y = step(h₁ − h₂ − 0.5). Test (0,0): h₁ = 0, h₂ = 0, y = step(−0.5) = 0. (0,1): h₁ = 1, h₂ = 0, y = step(0.5) = 1. (1,0): same, y = 1. (1,1): h₁ = 1, h₂ = 1, y = step(−0.5) = 0. XOR is correct.
chapters.trap: Depth counts the layers that carry weights, not the input layer; a 2–3–1 network is a two-layer network, not three. And a hidden layer is useless if its activation is linear, because two linear layers collapse into one.
chapters.leave: How the weights are trained is chapter 5.5; the activation σ itself is chapter 5.4.

chapters.idea: The activation function decides what each unit passes on and the loss function measures how wrong the output is, and both must be differentiable for training to work.
chapters.depth: Activation functions with their formulas, ranges and derivatives: step, sigmoid 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), tanh, ReLU max(0, z), leaky ReLU, softmax for multiclass. Say where each is used (sigmoid and tanh saturate, ReLU in hidden layers, softmax at the output). Loss functions: squared error for regression, binary cross-entropy −[t log y + (1−t) log(1−y)], categorical cross-entropy −Σ tᵢ log yᵢ with softmax, and hinge in one line. State why the derivative matters for chapter 5.5.

figure.aria: Three curves over z from minus 6 to 6 show the sigmoid flattening near 0 and 1, a steeper sigmoid flattening faster, and tanh flattening near minus 1 and 1.

chapters.example: Softmax and cross-entropy for 3 classes. Logits z = (2, 1, 0). e² = 7.389, e¹ = 2.718, e⁰ = 1, sum = 11.107. Probabilities: 7.389/11.107 = 0.665, 2.718/11.107 = 0.245, 1/11.107 = 0.090; they add to 1. If the true class is the first one, loss = −ln(0.665) = 0.408. If the true class were the third, loss = −ln(0.090) = 2.408, much larger.
chapters.trap: Sigmoid with binary cross-entropy for two classes, softmax with categorical cross-entropy for more than two; mixing them up gives a wrong loss. Write the loss over all classes, not just the true one, and remember ReLU is not differentiable at exactly 0.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.3 for where the functions sit, Unit 2 for the loss idea.
chapters.leave: Loss derivation and the bias-variance view are Unit 2; hinge loss is Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Backpropagation is the chain rule applied layer by layer backwards, giving the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight in one sweep.
chapters.depth: Full derivation for one hidden layer: forward z = Wx + b, a = σ(z), loss L; backward δ_output = ∂L/∂z, δ_hidden = (Wᵀδ) ⊙ σ′(z), then ∂L/∂W = δ a_prevᵀ and ∂L/∂b = δ. Define δ, the Hadamard product ⊙ and the Jacobian in one line. One worked numeric step, the update w ← w − η ∂L/∂w, and the cost of one pass. Mention computation graphs and that the same code handles any depth; name error back propagation as the older syllabus wording.

figure.title: Forward pass and backward gradient flow
figure.aria: Values flow down from input to loss, and dashed arrows climb back carrying the derivatives used to compute the weight gradients.

chapters.trap: Evaluate σ′ at the pre-activation z, not at the loss or the input, and multiply by a_prev when forming ∂L/∂W. Also keep the sign: gradient descent subtracts the gradient, so a negative gradient increases the weight.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 5.3 and 5.4; partial derivatives and the chain rule.
chapters.leave: Stochastic sampling of batches and the optimizers are chapter 5.6; plain gradient descent is Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Plain gradient descent is slow and overfits, so training uses better update rules (momentum, RMSProp, Adam) and penalties that keep weights small.
chapters.depth: Batch versus stochastic (SGD) versus mini-batch updates and why noise helps. Momentum v ← βv + g then w ← w − ηv; RMSProp as a one-line idea; Adam in formula form with its two moment estimates and bias correction, noting that only a few universities teach Adam's correction terms in detail. Regularization: L2 weight decay adding λ‖w‖² to the loss and its gradient 2λw, L1 for sparsity, early stopping, dropout with keep probability p and the test-time scaling, and batch normalization in a short block (normalize z, then scale and shift with γ, β) — flag that batch norm and Adam together are advanced for this unit. Hyper-parameter tuning: η, λ, layer widths, batch size, searched on a validation split.

figure.title: One mini-batch training step
figure.aria: A mini-batch goes through the forward pass and the penalised loss, gradients come back, an Adam step updates the weights, and the next batch repeats the cycle.

chapters.example: Momentum versus plain SGD. Weight starts at w = 1, η = 0.1, β = 0.9, and the gradient is g = 0.4 at each of three steps. Plain SGD: w = 1 − 0.04 = 0.96, then 0.92, then 0.88. Momentum: v₁ = 0.4, w = 1 − 0.1×0.4 = 0.96; v₂ = 0.9×0.4 + 0.4 = 0.76, w = 0.96 − 0.076 = 0.884; v₃ = 0.9×0.76 + 0.4 = 1.084, w = 0.884 − 0.1084 = 0.7756. Momentum covers more distance in the same three steps. Add L2 with λ = 0.01: at w = 2 the penalty is 0.01×2² = 0.04 and it adds 2×0.01×2 = 0.04 to the gradient.
chapters.trap: Regularize weights, not biases, and never tune λ or η on the test set. Dropout is switched off at prediction time (or the weights are rescaled once); leaving it on makes the output random.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.5 (needs the gradients), Unit 2 (overfitting, ridge and lasso).
chapters.leave: Cross-validation and the full evaluation toolkit are Unit 2; ensembling is Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Deep networks learn layered features, but sigmoid-type units saturate and the gradient shrinks towards zero, which ReLU and careful initialization fix.
chapters.depth: What depth buys: features composed from features (edges → parts → objects), and the difference in wording between an ANN and deep learning (many layers, learned representations rather than hand-built features, big data and GPUs). The vanishing gradient problem in full: each sigmoid factor is at most 0.25, so a product over layers decays fast; also the exploding case. ReLU and its variants as the fix, better initialization, residual connections in one line, and unit saturation as the older name. Only a few universities teach residual connections at this level.

figure.aria: The sigmoid chain curve falls steeply towards zero over ten layers while the ReLU chain stays flat at one.

chapters.example: Gradient reaching the first layer of a five-layer sigmoid network. If every layer gives the best-case derivative σ′(z) = 0.25, the factor after 5 layers is 0.25⁵ = 0.00098, so a first-layer gradient of 1.0 arrives as about 0.001. With ReLU and positive pre-activations the per-layer factor is 1, so the same gradient arrives as 1.0. A gradient of 0.001 against a learning rate of 0.1 moves the first-layer weight by only 0.0001 per step.
chapters.trap: Deep learning is not just more epochs or a bigger batch; it means more layers with learned features. And ReLU does not remove vanishing gradients everywhere — a unit stuck at z < 0 has zero gradient and never recovers on its own.
chapters.leave: Batch normalization and dropout details are chapter 5.6; the optimizer choice is also 5.6.

chapters.idea: A convolution slides a small shared filter over the input, and pooling shrinks the result, so a CNN learns from images with far fewer weights than a dense network.
chapters.depth: Convolution as a sliding dot product: output size floor((n + 2p − f)/s) + 1 with n input side, p padding, f filter side, s stride. Kernels as edge or blob detectors, weight sharing and local receptive fields as the reasons for the saving, number of parameters in a conv layer = f×f×channels_in×filters + filters. Pooling: max and average, size, stride, no parameters. Full pipeline: conv → ReLU → pool → flatten → dense → softmax, and name LeNet, AlexNet, VGG and ResNet in one line each with transfer learning mentioned briefly.

figure.title: CNN pipeline for one 5×5 input
figure.aria: A 5 by 5 input goes through a 3 by 3 convolution giving a 3 by 3 map, then ReLU, then 2 by 2 max pooling giving 2 by 2, then flattening and softmax.

chapters.trap: Use the output-size formula with the floor, and remember a filter's depth must equal the input's channel count. Pooling has no weights, and a 3×3 conv on a 5×5 input does not give a 5×5 output.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 5.4 (ReLU, softmax), 5.5 (how filters get trained), 5.7 (why deep stacks work).
chapters.leave: The full architecture details of ResNet and transfer learning are touched only in one line; clustering in the same syllabus is Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A recurrent network keeps a hidden state that carries information across time steps, which lets it handle sequences of any length with one shared set of weights.
chapters.depth: Recurrent unit: h_t = tanh(W x_t + U h_{t−1} + b), output y_t = V h_t. Unrolling over time, weight sharing across steps, and backpropagation through time (BPTT) in outline. Vanishing and exploding gradients over long sequences and gradient clipping. LSTM in enough detail for an exam: cell state, forget gate f_t = σ(W_f[h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_f), input gate, output gate, and how the additive cell state carries gradient; GRU in one line. Uses: language models, speech, time series, and the sequence labelling behind next-word prediction on a phone keyboard.

figure.title: One recurrent step
figure.aria: The previous hidden state and the current input combine in a weighted sum with tanh to give the new hidden state, which produces the output and feeds the next step.

chapters.example: Two steps with W = 0.5, U = 0.5, b = 0, h₀ = 0, x₁ = x₂ = 1. Step 1: net = 0.5×1 + 0.5×0 = 0.5, h₁ = tanh(0.5) = 0.462. Step 2: net = 0.5×1 + 0.5×0.462 = 0.731, h₂ = tanh(0.731) = 0.624. Gradient factors: ∂h₂/∂h₁ = U(1 − h₂²) = 0.5 × (1 − 0.389) = 0.306; ∂h₁/∂h₀ = 0.5 × (1 − 0.214) = 0.393. Over just two steps the product is 0.120; after ten such steps it is below 0.0001, which is why long sequences lose the early signal.
chapters.trap: The same W, U, V are reused at every time step, so the parameter count does not grow with sequence length. Do not say BPTT is a different algorithm from backpropagation — it is backpropagation on the unrolled graph.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 5.5 and 5.7 (chain rule, vanishing gradients), 5.4 (tanh and sigmoid).
chapters.leave: Reinforcement learning with states and rewards is Unit 6; sequence models are not revisited.
